title: Internal or External Ideals: The Hero or the Victim
author: Patrick Whalen
summary: Patrick Whalen develops an extended argument about two fundamental orientations to life: the internal ideal of the hero, who locates the standard of excellence within himself and treats every challenge as an opportunity to prove and develop his character; and the external ideal of the victim, who locates causation and responsibility outside himself and responds to difficulty with excuse, avoidance, and blame. The article works through multiple domains — physicality, spirituality, family, friendship, politics, and culture — to show how the heroic orientation transforms suffering into material for growth while the victim orientation uses suffering as evidence that the world has wronged it. The piece is explicitly philosophical and aspirational, drawing on classical heroic ideals rather than pop-psychology reframes: the hero does not deny pain but gathers it as the raw material for an interior monument. Whalen presents victimhood as a choice rather than a circumstance, and heroism as a demanding but always-available alternative orientation that does not depend on outcomes.
points: The hero holds standards internally — derived from an ideal of what he can become — which means he cannot ultimately be disappointed by anyone but himself. The victim holds standards externally, which means every setback can be attributed to forces beyond his control.

Challenge and difficulty, for the hero, are the preconditions of excellence rather than evidence of victimization. The hero is 'joyful in the face of challenge, takes responsibility and avoids casting blame, and is vigorous in doing whatever it is that needs to be done.'

The heroic orientation applies across domains: in physicality (extraordinary discipline in the face of physical suffering or illness), in spirituality (a powerful love that gathers loss and privation as material for interior growth), in family and friendship, and in civic and cultural engagement.
Victim spirituality cannot recognize joy or sustain the losses that inevitably accompany human love; heroic spirituality gathers pain and builds something from it rather than being defined by it.

The ideals the hero holds for himself are deliberately high — 'delightfully high, impossibly high' — because ideals exist as aspirational poles, not as performance targets. Placing them high enough that we must reach is the point of having them.
quotes: The hero is joyful in the face of challenge, takes responsibility and avoids casting blame, and is vigorous in doing whatever it is that needs to be done. The hero's standards for himself or for herself are extremely high. Delightfully high. You might even think impossibly high. But after all, we're talking about ideals. Let's place them high enough that we have to reach a little.

Heroic physicality would look something like extraordinary physical discipline, dignified bearing, efforts toward cultivating beauty in your person and surroundings, and vigorous exercise and fitness. Physical suffering — whether self-imposed, or on account of illness or aging — can be considered an opportunity for soul and body alike to show their mettle.
The victim mentality, on the other hand, is one that looks for a way out, that makes excuses, and that dodges accountability.

Heroic spirituality would look like a powerful love of God, one's neighbor, and a voracious search for wisdom. The loss of a loved one would be a trial which opens new vistas of understanding — makes each minute of life and each friend and loved one even more precious.
Gathering that pain and privation as the raw materials to construct an interior monument, which builds up and ennobles while it marks the loss.
Challenge is where I have the opportunity to prove my mettle. The precondition for excellence. Challenge is where the hero shows what he is made of, rather than what the world has done to him.
